Plan: diagnose DNS propagation and caching; inspect CoreDNS ConfigMap, adjust TTL if needed, refresh caches, and enact a controlled canary rollout of the DNS changes. Commands: kubectl -n kcsa-prod ge
Configure both MutatingAdmissionWebhook and ValidatingAdmissionWebhook with failurePolicy: Fail so requests are rejected if the webhook is unavailable.

Run: kubectl top pods -n kcsa-prod; kubectl logs -n kcsa-prod -l app=data-processor --tail=200; kubectl exec -n kcsa-prod <producer-pod> -- kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server broker-0.kafka:9092

questions.explanation:
## Correct Answer
A. Setting failurePolicy to Fail ensures requests are rejected when a webhook is unavailable, avoiding silent acceptance or partial mutations during webhook outages.

## Why Other Options Are Wrong
- B is incorrect because Ignore can allow potentially unsafe requests when the webhook is down, increasing risk.
- C is incorrect because removing webhooks reduces policy enforcement and could violate compliance requirements.
- D is incorrect because a 300-second timeout would stall requests and degrade availability; a safety-first approach uses fail-closed behavior with reasonable timeouts.

## Key Concepts
- Admission webhooks can mutate or validate requests; their availability should be treated as a safety hinge.
- failurePolicy controls how the API server behaves when a webhook is unreachable.

## Real-World Application
- In production, ensure webhooks fail closed to prevent potentially unsafe changes when webhook services are temporarily unavailable, preserving cluster integrity.

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical debugging skills for service mesh configurations under load, with emphasis on rate-limiting diagnostics, Envoy introspection, and safe policy rollouts while maintaining latency SLAs.

## Key Concepts
- Istio rate limiting and quota management
- Envoy proxy-config tooling for introspection
- Canary deployments and gradual traffic shifting
- End-to-end latency metrics (P95)

## Code Example
```bash
# Inspect gateway pods
kubectl -n kcsa-prod get pods -l app=gateway

# Get gateway pod name
POD=$(kubectl -n kcsa-prod get pod -l app=gateway -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

# View Envoy cluster configuration
istioctl proxy-config cluster $POD -n kcsa-prod

# View Envoy route configuration
istioctl proxy-config route $POD -n kcsa-prod

# Check Envoy stats for rate limiting
istioctl proxy-config stats $POD -n kcsa-prod | grep ratelimit

# Apply updated rate limit configuration
kubectl apply -f rate-limit-config.yaml -n kcsa-prod

# Verify canary deployment
kubectl get pods -n kcsa-prod -l version=canary
```

## Why This Is Asked

## Code Example
```javascript
// DestinationRule snippet (per-tenant circuit-breaker)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: tenant-cb
  namespace: kcsa-prod
spec:
  host: "*.svc.cluster.local"
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 100
        maxConnections: 1000
    outlierDetection:
      consecutiveErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
```
```javascript
// VirtualService canary routing (10% to canary)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: gateway-virtual
  namespace: kcsa-prod
spec:
  hosts:
  - gateway.example.com
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: tenant-api
        subset: v1
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: tenant-api
        subset: v1-canary

```
